title: Satisfiability of Equality Equations
statement: Each string in `equations` has exactly four characters and states a relation between two variables named by single lowercase letters: `"x==y"` says that `x` and `y` are equal, and `"x!=y"` says that they differ. The two letters may be the same. Return `true` if some assignment of integers to the letters makes every relation in the list hold at once, and `false` if no such assignment exists.
constraints: equations[i][0] and equations[i][3] are lowercase letters
notes:
## Intuition

Equality is transitive: if `a==b` and `b==c`, then `a` and `c` must hold the same number even though no equation links them directly. The `==` equations therefore split the letters into groups that are forced to be equal, and giving each group its own distinct integer satisfies every `==`. The only way to fail is a `!=` whose two letters landed in the same group. Union-find builds those groups in near-constant time per equation. A slower alternative keeps spreading labels across `==` edges until nothing changes.

## Approach

1. Give each of the 26 letters its own set: `parent[i] = i`.
2. `find(x)` follows parents up to the set's root, halving the path as it goes.
3. First pass: for every `==` equation, join the two letters' sets by pointing one root at the other.
4. Second pass: for every `!=` equation, if both letters have the same root they are forced equal, so return `false`.
5. If no `!=` conflicts, return `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

`equations = ["a==b", "b!=a"]`. First pass: `"a==b"` gives `left = 0` and `right = 1`; both are roots, so `parent[0] = 1`. Second pass: `"b!=a"` gives `left = 1`, `right = 0`; `find(1) = 1` and `find(0)` follows `parent[0]` to `1`. The roots match, so the answer is `false`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · α(26)), effectively O(n): two passes, each with a couple of nearly constant `find` calls.
- Space: O(1): the `parent` array always has 26 entries.

## Pitfalls

- Do all `==` merges before checking any `!=`. One combined pass would accept `["a!=c","a==b","b==c"]`, because `a` and `c` are joined only after the `!=` was checked.
- Join the roots, `parent[find(left)] = find(right)`, not the letters themselves; `parent[left] = right` would cut `left` off from its earlier group.
- `"a!=a"` can never hold. It needs no special case, because a letter always shares its own root.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `parent` | `parent[i]`: the next letter up in `i`'s set; a root points to itself |
| `find` | returns the root of a letter's set |
| `x` | the letter `find` is currently at |
| `equation` | the relation being read |
| `left`, `right` | the two letters as indices 0 to 25 |

narration.2: Each of the 26 letters starts alone in its own set.
narration.4: find returns the root letter that represents x's set.
narration.5: Climb until reaching a letter that is its own parent, the root.
narration.6: Path halving: point x at its grandparent so later searches are shorter.
narration.12: First pass: build the groups from the equalities only.
narration.14: Turn the first letter into an index from 0 to 25.
narration.15: Turn the second letter into an index the same way.
narration.16: Join the two sets by hanging one root under the other.
narration.20: Second pass: every equality is merged, so the groups are final.
narration.21: Now look only at the '!=' equations.
narration.24: Both letters are forced to be equal, so this inequality cannot hold.
narration.27: No inequality conflicts with the groups, so giving each group its own integer works.
